people.title: People and Genealogy
people.timelineCaptionHistorical: Lifespans on the historical (BCE/CE) timeline. Dates are scholarly approximations.
people.regionsByTextSafeguard: Restricted to regions and peoples the biblical text itself names. Per the anti-misuse safeguards in Genesis 9 and 10, this section MUST NOT be read as descent claims about modern peoples or nations. See chapter companions for the full safeguards.
people.lead: Genealogical data is drawn from the Masoretic Text. Birth and death years are calculated from the text's own internal arithmetic — Anno Mundi, the year from creation. Where the text gives no figure, the profile says "not stated."
people.leadGeneric: Figures named in the text, with the fields the source records. All claims are labelled by type and confidence; "not stated" where the text is silent.
people.timelineCaption: Bars span each figure's lifespan in years from creation (AM). The dashed bar is Chanokh (Enoch), "taken" at 365. By the text's own arithmetic, every generation from Adam to Lamech was still alive when Noah was born — and the Flood (AM 1656) falls the year Methuselah dies.

landing.languageTagline: The Bible → English · Português · Deutsch · Español
landing.differenceDesc: The same verse. One hides the choices. The other shows them.
landing.conventionalVerse: Now the serpent was more crafty than any of the wild animals the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden'?"
landing.transparentVerse: And the serpent was *arum* (crafty/shrewd) from all the living things of the field that YHWH God had made. And it said to the woman: "Indeed, *did* God say, 'You shall not eat from any tree of the garden'?"
landing.diff1: The Hebrew says YHWH — four consonants, no vowels. Most Bibles swap it for 'the LORD.' We put back what was there.
landing.diff2: The word for 'crafty' (*arum*) sounds almost identical to 'naked' (*arom*) from the verse before. The author did that on purpose. Most translations erase it.
landing.diff3: The serpent exaggerates the rule. The woman corrects it — but quietly changes the original command too. We keep both distortions visible.
landing.diff4: Every word in italics was added to make English work. It is not in the Hebrew. You always know what is original and what is scaffolding.
landing.howReading: The full story as flowing prose on a clean page. No footnotes, no interruptions. Just you and the text.
landing.howStudy: The Hebrew behind every word, where we made choices, and why. Verse by verse, color-coded.
landing.who1: You *believe* — and you want to meet the text as it was actually written, before centuries of translation smoothed it over.
landing.who2: You *doubt*, or follow another path entirely — and you are willing to be surprised by what the originals actually say.
landing.who3: You *study* these texts and want a translation that shows its work: every choice visible, every uncertainty admitted.
landing.scope: This one shows you exactly where — in English, Portuguese, German, and Spanish. It is not a devotional. It is not a replacement for scholarly editions. It is a disciplined attempt to let you see what is actually there.
landing.scopeNot: When we don't know something, we say so. When scholars disagree, we show you both sides.
landing.rulesPageSubtitle: The governance system behind the Transparent Translation.
landing.rulesIntro: Every translation makes choices. Most hide them. We wrote ours down.
landing.rulesPrimeDesc: If any rule conflicts with these four principles, the principles win.
landing.rulesPrime1: If the original text is *complex*, we keep it complex.
landing.rulesPrime2: If the original text is *ambiguous*, we keep it ambiguous.
landing.rulesPrime3: We do not *add* words the source text does not say — unless the target language physically cannot form a sentence without them.
landing.rulesPrime4: When we do add a word, we *mark* it so you can see it.
landing.rule1short: Same source word → same translation, by default.
landing.rule1example: Hebrew אֶרֶץ (*eretz*) always → **land**. Greek ἐκκλησία (*ekklesia*) → **assembly**, not “church.”
landing.rule2short: If source text supports two meanings, preserve both.
landing.rule3short: Don't sneak in later concepts not in the source text.
landing.rule3example: Hebrew: **sky**, not ‘Heaven.’ Greek: **assembly**, not ‘church.’ **Good news**, not ‘Gospel.’
landing.rule4short: Transliterate when translation would impose a single reading.
landing.rule5short: Core terms locked across the project.
landing.rule6short: When traditions conflict, source text governs.
landing.rule7short: Repeated phrases rendered identically each time.
landing.rule8short: Preserve tense, aspect, and voice from source.
landing.rule11short: Mark every word not in the source text.
landing.rule11example: “And God saw that *it was* good” — italics show ‘it was’ is added for English grammar.
landing.rule12short: Preserve source sentence structure where possible.
landing.rule13short: Flag debated terms with confidence labels.
landing.rule14short: Note sound patterns and textual echoes.
landing.rule15short: Translation must work when read aloud.
landing.rule16short: All 4 target languages render the same source consistently.
landing.rule17short: Same source passage → same rendering across books.
landing.rule19short: When rules conflict, explicit priority order applies.
landing.rule21short: Commentary belongs in notes, not in translation.
landing.rule22short: Translate base text; note variants, don't adopt silently.
landing.rule23short: Respect the genre of each passage.
landing.rule24short: Transparent vs Reader edition, declared explicitly.
landing.rule25example: **YHWH** — because that is what the Hebrew consonants are. The vowels were never written.
landing.rule26short: Significant variants noted in companion material.
landing.rule28short: No verse ships without documented review.
landing.rule29short: Companion material in separate files, labeled by type and confidence.
landing.howDeeper: Historical and linguistic background, prophecy readings, and the people behind the text — each labeled by claim type and confidence.

start.title: Start here
start.lead: New to these texts? This is the gentlest way in — a path that starts with the heart and ends at the beginning.
start.why: Most people open to page one and give up by chapter twenty. So don’t start there. Begin with the Psalms — raw human feeling. Then Proverbs for how to live, and Ecclesiastes for what it all means; read a little of each side by side. Then meet the figure who reframed everything in the Gospels, follow the movement he left behind, and end with its vision of how the story closes. Only then go back to Genesis — the beginning — and read how it all started.
start.interleaveNote: Read one of each, side by side, until the Psalms are done.
